cells.tense: The work is in your hands today and you're the one holding it.
cells.ask: Next time you start, name one wish inside the practise you'd keep if only one could stay, and let that be the whole goal for the session.
cells.core:
The same small set of moves, done again and again, has stopped being a rehearsal for something later. The spark that catches at the start isn't a phase before the real thing.

An open mind is what keeps this from going stiff. When a new hunger comes up in the middle of it — an itch to try one more variation, to look at a move you've done a thousand times as if it were new — that's a beginning asking for something. Holding the moves you know and the fresh want that hasn't found its shape, at the same time, keeps the work alive instead of settling into habit. Naming the wish is how the two stay neighbours.
cells.sheetLine: The beginning you keep meeting is the work, not the wait for it.
cells.verb: letting a first spark catch and seeing what it wants to be
cells.place: the room where the same thing gets done over and over until it's clean

cells.tense: You're a few moves ahead of yourself, in a session that hasn't happened yet.
cells.ask: Before the next session, write one sentence on what you want the practise to become, close the notebook, and start with no plan for how it gets there.
cells.core:
Somewhere up there is the shape it's supposed to take — what it should look like when it's working, what it should be by the time you're done — and you're trying to start from that picture instead of from the spark you actually have. A beginning is small and unlit. It won't carry the weight of where you think it's going.

The practise, kept honest, is a small light you keep lit by attention, not by force. You show up, do the repetition, and let the shape come out of the repetition rather than out of a plan you brought. Staying clear means seeing what's on the bench today rather than the finished thing you're imagining. The gap between the version you want and the version you have is just information. Starting from where the spark actually is gets you further than skipping to the end of it.
cells.sheetLine: You're trying to start from a finished thing instead of a beginning.

cells.tense: You're at the door of the practise, and the door has been open for a while.
cells.ask: Before the next time you'd normally sit down with it, tell one person one true thing about why this work matters to you, and let that be the whole of it.
cells.core:
You know the shape of a session, the feel of the repetition, the small quiet that shows up when you're inside it. Most days, still, you don't walk through. What's gone quiet isn't how to do it. It's the showing up.

What's missing isn't more discipline — the discipline is the room you already built. It's the link between the work and anything outside it. When someone has the practise and not the hours, a finished session leaves them more whole rather than more behind; it feels like being in contact with something, the way you'd be in contact with a person. Forcing the room to feel full doesn't work. Touching the part of you that already knows why this matters is what pulls you back through the door.
cells.sheetLine: The work is still there. What's gone quiet is the reason you'd walk toward it.

cells.tense: The practise runs even in the hours you'd file under not-practising.
cells.ask: Pick one moment today you'd normally file under 'not really the work' — the walk, the washing-up, an idle minute — and write one sentence about what it's feeding in the practise.
cells.core:
Something in you is refining all day long — noticing how a thing got done, wanting the next attempt a little cleaner, turning a small moment over because it caught you. Then when you talk about the work, you point to the scheduled session and call the rest off the clock. The refining is happening. The saying-so isn't.

When the practising person knows what they're doing, the practise isn't a box on a calendar. It's a way the whole day is arranged, quietly, without announcement — the same attention you'd bring to a session, showing up in how you hold a cup or how you listen to someone. The beginning you keep meeting isn't only in the formal hour. It's the small fresh moments scattered through the day. Naming one of them as part of the work doesn't make you grander. It stops you pretending the part of you already doing this isn't yours.
cells.sheetLine: You're already practising. You're just putting it down to something else.

attempts.check: The risk is over-claiming: the core saying the person already has a practise asking to exist, when the cards only say a beginning is present in what they know how to do. A reader could reasonably object that they are still at the very start and there is nothing to be heard yet, or that they cannot choose what asks to be noticed. The asks survive being wrong because they each produce a result the person can see — a craving named, a wish written down, a smaller next session — regardless of whether the read about capacity is accurate. The sentence serving the writer most is the Balanced sheetLine, which is clean but slightly too self-congratulating; it should be balanced by the core's final turn, which is about hearing rather than deserving.
